blocks.text: Chapter 6.
Bayes's Rule: Predicting from Almost Nothing
Sixth night, friend — and it begins in 1969, with a young physicist on vacation, staring up at the Berlin Wall.

His name is J. Richard Gott the Third. The Wall is eight years old — a slab of concrete politics that could stand for a century or fall next spring. Gott knows nothing about East German politburo dynamics, nothing about Soviet intentions. One observation: the Wall is eight years old. And from that single fact, he makes a prediction about when it will fall.

Twenty years later, friend, the Wall came down — inside Gott's predicted window. Tonight: the 250-year-old formula that turns one glance into a rational forecast, the three secret families every quantity in your life belongs to... and the place where the modern world quietly poisons the machine.
One data point and a prior

The mathematics starts with Thomas Bayes — an eighteenth-century minister whose great essay was published only after his death, in 1763. His insight: to reason backward from evidence, imagine every hidden cause that could have produced what you see, weight each by how likely it was to do so... and by how plausible it was before you looked. That last piece is the prior — and it isn't cheating, friend; it's required. Win a raffle on your only ticket: what fraction of tickets are winners? Without some assumption about raffles in general, one winning ticket tells you nothing. Laplace completed the mathematics and left us a jewel for tiny samples — Laplace's Law: after w successes in n tries, estimate the odds as (w+1)/(n+2). One win in one try? Not 100% — two-thirds. The formula quietly adds one imaginary success and one imaginary failure, protecting you from absurd overconfidence while still learning from every observation. Laplace ran it on the sunrise itself: given all recorded history, the odds of the sun rising tomorrow are overwhelming... but formally, never quite certain. That's Bayesian humility, friend: evidence updates belief — it never replaces it.

Pause and guess: Now, Gott at the Wall. His only assumption: "my visit is not a special moment — I'm equally likely to be seeing this thing at any point in its life." From that alone, what's the prediction — and how did it fare against history?
Ready? Here is what happened.

On average, an unremarkable visitor arrives at the halfway mark — so expect the thing to last as long again as it already has. Total lifespan: double the current age. The Wall was eight years old, so Gott guessed roughly eight more years — with a 50%-confidence window from one-third to three times the observed age. It fell twenty years later, comfortably inside the window, and Gott published the method in Nature, applying it to Broadway shows and the survival of the human species. He called it the Copernican Principle — nothing privileged about your vantage point, just as Copernicus dethroned the Earth. But here's the deep truth, friend: the doubling rule is simply Bayes's Rule run with an uninformative prior — the prior of total ignorance about scale. That explains its failures too: meet a 90-year-old and doubling predicts he'll live to 180; meet a 6-year-old and it predicts death at 12. Absurd — because you know things about human lifespans. You have a rich, well-shaped prior... and when you have one, Bayes commands you to use it. The right prediction rule depends entirely on the prior's shape.

And shapes come in three great families. Power-law quantities — town populations, wealth, movie grosses — sprawl across scales with rare giants; the rule is multiply: a film at $6 million so far ends near $8.4 million (empirical factor ~1.4), and the longer such a thing has lasted, the longer it will last. Normal quantities — lifespans, heights — cluster around an average; the rule is predict the mean, or a whisker past it once you've exceeded it: the 6-year-old reaches ~77, the 90-year-old ~94. And Erlang quantities — waits between independent events, a politician's tenure, a gambler's streak — are memoryless; the rule is add a constant: always the same expected span remaining, no matter the history. Three families, three opposite intuitions, friend: the rich get richer... the old die sooner... and the streak's age means nothing. Knowing which world you're in is the whole game.
The Bayesians in your head

Do ordinary people actually compute like this? Tom Griffiths — this book's co-author — and Josh Tenenbaum tested it: single-datum questions like a movie has grossed $10 million so far; total? — a man is 39; lifespan? — a congressman has served 11 years; total tenure? The 2006 results were stunning: people's median answers tracked the Bayes-optimal predictions almost exactly — including the switches between rules. Multiplying for movies, averaging for lifespans, adding for tenures. Nobody did arithmetic, friend. The correct priors, absorbed from a lifetime of movies and obituaries and elections, were simply in them. The one revealing miss: Egyptian pharaohs — right rule, wrong data, because people assumed ancient reigns resembled modern ones, when pharaohs took thrones young and died young. Flawless machinery, corrupted inputs. Hold that phrase.

Pause and guess: Because corrupted inputs reframe one of psychology's most famous experiments: Mischel's marshmallow test — kids who resisted one marshmallow to earn a second later thrived, and "willpower" got the credit. In 2012, Celeste Kidd added ONE thing to the experiment before the marshmallow appeared. What — and what happened to the willpower story?
Ready? Here is what happened.

She had the adult keep or break a small promise first — better art supplies, promised and then delivered... or promised and not. Children who'd just watched the adult prove unreliable waited only about three minutes before eating the marshmallow. Children with the reliable adult waited around twelve — most lasting the entire test. Because waiting is only rational, friend, if you believe the second marshmallow will actually arrive — a Bayesian judgment about adult reliability. The child who grabs the treat may not lack self-control; she may have accurate priors about a world where promised rewards don't come. Failing the test can be optimal inference from hard experience — which means the intervention that matters is the child's environment, not her willpower. And the same warning lands on you nightly: your brain builds priors from the frequency of what it encounters, and news media report events because they are rare — plane crashes over car crashes, murders over heart disease. Consume enough and your internal statistics drift from reality; risk-perception studies show people overestimate exactly the vivid deaths that get coverage. Everything you take in is training data for your future predictions, friend. Protect the diet, and you protect the machine.
Before you go

So: one data point plus a prior beats no prediction at all; Laplace's (w+1)/(n+2) keeps you humble at tiny samples; Gott doubled the Wall's age and history obliged; power-law multiplies, normal averages, Erlang adds — and knowing the family is the game; your intuitions are nearly perfect Bayesian engines... running on whatever data life fed them; and the marshmallow was never about willpower. This week, friend: audit the information diet — cut one stream that over-serves the rare and dramatic, and the forecasts you don't even know you're making will quietly improve.

But there's a shadow side to all this learning from data, friend — a trap that catches the most diligent thinkers hardest. Tomorrow: why the nine-factor model loses to the rule of thumb; why more thinking, more data, and more detail can make predictions worse; why evolution gave you tastebuds instead of nutritional spreadsheets — and when the smartest move is, mathematically, to think less. Next time: overfitting.
Key takeaways
One observation plus a prior yields a rational forecast — without a prior, a single data point means nothing.
Laplace's Law for tiny samples: (w+1)/(n+2) — one win in one try is two-thirds, never certainty.
Gott's Copernican doubling is Bayes with total ignorance: expect things to last as long again as they already have.
Three families, three rules: power-law → multiply; normal → predict the average; Erlang → add a constant, history irrelevant.
Humans are near-optimal Bayesians with good data — the pharaoh miss proves the failure mode is inputs, not machinery.
Protect your priors: media over-serves the rare and vivid, and the marshmallow test measured children's priors about adults, not willpower.
